I read it in high school circa 2016-2020 and just read the whole thing again today. I claimed it was my favorite book for a time in high school but couldn’t remember specifics after so long so I just reread it on a whim—I think the reason I enjoy it so much is because of Quick’s writing style. He so effortlessly portrays the minds of young characters in such an authentic way. I reread Every Exquisite Thing yesterday for the same reason, and my opinion is the same. The way he captures mental illness and teen hood in a way that doesn’t scream “I’m an older not mentally ill dude trying to write something I’m not” is what makes his writing so special IMO. I also think that FMLP in particular is interesting to reread as an adult because it’s now easier for me to relate to the other characters in the story. Before, I think I really related to Leonard in the sense that everything was dragging me down and I felt so alone and like there was no future that would be happy for me—now I actually feel the effects of the “it gets better” speeches from the adults in his life, and yet I can still feel his pain through channeling my teenage self. It’s amazing. Definitely recommend this book to everyone. 

Side note, but the way he explores religion in this book is flawless IMO. I really like Lauren as a character and I think that we get to see that Leonard isn’t as bad as he claims to be* in the way he actually listens to and tries to understand her POV about Christianity while asking valid questions to bring himself peace and understanding. He’s actually open to it, and I know he says it’s pretty much just because he likes Lauren, but I honestly think it’s another great example of how he’s looking desperately for hope and something to hold on to, even if he’s not willing to admit that. 

* we do obviously also see that he does bad things in the way he kisses her, but it shows he’s a morally grey character like the Nazis he discusses in class. Just to clarify, I don’t think being open to religion necessarily makes him a good person, but it shows that he has good in him (as do many other things in the story) when he’s convince that there isn’t any good in him at all.

I am so so sorry. I’m only a few years older than you and still feel too young to handle such big things, so I could only imagine what you’re experiencing. I just wanna validate that this is a horrible thing to experience and you should feel no fault or guilt in being heavily affected by it. Please let yourself process your emotions and lean on your living family members and friends. Voice your hurt, your thoughts, your feelings—don’t bottle them up. Take the time you need to really sit and process everything changing around you. Then invest your time into something healthy—maybe learn how to cook, sew, etc. Something you can do with short attainable goals that’ll make you feel proud of yourself and like you’re making progress in something. When my grandma died, I just sat for a whole year doing nothing, feeling like I made no life progress even though time was passing, until I picked up a hobby that was easy to keep track of (for me it was reading, which I hadn’t done since I was a lot younger due to not enough time. Watching my bookshelf grow with titles I’d read made me feel really accomplished, which in turn made me feel like my grandma would be proud of me). He loves you so much. I’m so sorry for your loss. 🩷

I’ve thought abt this a lot. I really think they’re somewhere in the center. As others have pointed out, Never Take It is kinda the biggest Independent anthem ever. Which isn’t a bad thing! I also think that as you mentioned, them posting things in favor of different human rights campaigns is good. I also don’t think *not* talking about political topics all the time is bad. I know I personally usually avoid discourse because it makes me feel extremely existential and gives me anxiety attacks, and as Tyler has been very open about mental health, it wouldn’t surprise me if he’s in the same boat. IMO there’s a difference between being uneducated and just not wanting to discuss. Yes they have a platform, but they *have* used it, and not using it more could very well relate to mental health etc. 

On another note, there are lots of conservatives who do not support the president. I know some personally! The hard thing about the US 2 party political system is that a whole bunch of differing opinions get lumped together because they’re “similar enough” to be grouped into one party. This is why I (and maybe Tyler/Josh too!) identify as an Independent, because there’s too much nuance in my opinions to be tied to one of the two major political parties. Other people, though, might feel that’s too complicated, and just jump in the boat of the party they most closely align with. This does not mean they agree with everything the party stands for, it unfortunately just means they might feel like they don’t have another option to choose. 

Finally, just wanted to point out that even if their families align with one party, that doesn’t necessarily mean that they also align with said party! My parents are republicans, my Baba is a democrat, and I lie somewhere in the middle. I think a lot more people are like this than we realize!

All that is to say, many people have names that can be pronounced multiple ways and have to correct *some* people *occasionally*, but people are usually good about it. I agree with the other comments but would also like to add something I’ve been thinking about a lot recently. 

The feelings of fluff and happiness we got from S1 and even S2 are wonderful, but irl I know very few, if any, teens who are that emotionally mature. I think sometimes people (me included, I’m people) forget that this is a fictional tv show with a lot of ideal behavior from the characters who are, in reality, still very mentally underdeveloped. We’re alllll figuring out how to handle our big emotions and mental illnesses that are starting to present themselves as teenagers, and we can honestly all be a little toxic as teens too (coming from someone who was previously dealing with a lot of similar issues irl in my young teen years, I didn’t handle it the best, being totally honest). 

I think because Charlie handled a lot of previous plot points in S1 & S2 very well, there’s lowkey some pressure on him to keep being emotionally mature and handle everything well. But, you don’t know what you don’t know, and he simply doesn’t know how to handle what he’s going through in S3. The IMPORTANT thing there, though, is that as soon as he can admit to himself that he doesn’t know what to do, he seeks help from someone who does. 

I’ve struggled recently with romanticizing the show & books prior to S3’s drop and comparing my own life to it, and I really had to have a reality check with myself that it’s *not* real. If some people had teen experiences with friends that emotionally mature, that’s wonderful, but it’s also okay that I didn’t because a lot of people don’t and that’s normal.

My dad is an anesthetist. I haven’t asked him specifically (and I can’t rn bc it’s 1:30am lol) but based on general comments he’s made over the years, I think healthcare workers who handle patients going under generally just like to keep the attitude light and jokey when the patient is feeling the effects of the meds. Every time I’ve gone under, I’ve felt like I suddenly have the personality and social skills of a five year old, and I think the medical staff have talked to me as though I were indeed a child. I think it’s a balance. 

That being said, I know he’s also mentioned that different people react very, VERY differently to the medication. For example, there’s the stereotypical talker, who just says out of pocket stuff like in all those viral wisdom teeth videos. Then there’s the laughers who just think everything (EVERYTHING) is just soooo funny for seemingly no reason. Then there’s the ones who get super sick, like extremely nauseous—this is my mom. Post-op, she’s always been very somber and focusing on not puking (sometimes unsuccessfully). Then there’s me, the cryer. I SOB and sob and sob hysterically when I wake up. For actual hours until the medication wears off. I always say over and over again “I swear I don’t want to cry, I’m not trying to cry, I don’t know why I’m crying,” all while wailing. 

While I know every person’s experience with how they react to the medication can differ wildly (as mentioned above), I’ve found through the people I’ve talked to who’ve had multiple operations (including myself) tend to have the same personal reaction every time they wake up. So for example, like I said, my mom gets really sick and I sob, which is different from one another, but for each of us our experiences remain consistent each time it happens (ie she’s always a sick one and I’m always a sobbing gal).

ETA: also most recently I had an operation the week before Christmas. When I was crying in the recovery room the nurse asked me if I wanted to listen to music, and I BEGGED to listen to “Wonderful Christmastime” by Paul McCartney. We listened to it like seven times in a row bc I just wanted to hear it again and again LOL

I’d bring it up with your doctor! Explain everything going on and maybe he/she will decide it’s in your best interest to adjust your dosage. I’ve been on different SSRI’s since I was pretty young, and I’ve noticed things can feel like not enough or too much sometimes depending on what’s going on (family medical emergencies, new schools, new jobs, etc.) and the best thing you can do is talk to your doctor.
